items.title: How the Culture War Put Public Schools at Risk
items.description: For more than half a century after Milton Friedman proposed using taxpayer money to support students in private schools, the libertarian economist’s idea went almost nowhere. Republican presidents, including Ronald Reagan and George W. Bush, pushed vouchers—which help parents enroll their children in schools of their choice, including private and religious schools, at taxpayer expense — as a way to liberate poor children from failing big-city school districts. Those efforts led to voucher initiatives in a smattering of districts, such as Cleveland, Milwaukee, and Washington, D.C. But in state after state, support for public schools—which take all comers and have historically played a crucial role in cultivating students’ common identity as Americans—was just too broad-based and too strong to get voucherlike programs approved on a larger scale. In the past several years, though, voucher advocates have switched strategies to take advantage of the country’s ever-deepening political polarization. In 2022, the Heritage Foundation urged the voucher movement “to embrace the culture war” as a way of promoting school choice. As evidence of progressive overreach, the conservative think tank has pointed to “racial essentialism for third graders” and decried the presence in some school libraries of Gender Queer , a graphic novel that “features a picture of oral sex being performed on a sex toy.” Conservative leaders in many state capitals have emulated Heritage’s tactics, and the tactical shift has helped persuade lawmakers to expand the supply of school vouchers. Amy Sinclair, the president of the Iowa state Senate, told an interviewer in 2023 that during the coronavirus pandemic, “many parents became aware of anti-American and explicit materials in their child’s classrooms and began to demand choice.” “There’s no reason why any students should have a woke agenda pushed on them,” Texas Governor Greg Abbott declared a month later at a rally for private-school-choice legislation. The following year, his Arkansas counterpart, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, promoted her school-choice efforts by declaring on X , “We need kids learning math, reading, and science—not woke nonsense.” Since the pandemic, voucherlike programs have proliferated, and they are now open to even the richest students. In 2021, no states had universal programs supporting private education with public dollars; by 2025, 18 did. The number of students using publicly funded private-school-choice programs has tripled since the 2018–19 school year. [ Idrees Kahloon: Nikole Hannah-Jones faced too much apathy to win ] The problem for traditional public schools is that some districts have left themselves open to the political critique that Heritage has been promoting: Many school systems have become identified with progressive causes and have neglected their role as a unifying force in American society. Out of a sincere concern for social justice, they have embraced ideas about diversity, inclusion, and anti-racism that, when applied in practice, prove off-putting even for some liberals. Sixty-eight percent of American adults agreed with the 2023 U.S. Supreme Court decision striking down racial preferences in higher education. But many educators have flocked toward the books of Ibram X. Kendi—whose approach toward “anti-racism” insists that “the only remedy to past discrimination is present discrimination”—and related ideas emanating from education schools. In a 2025 poll , 58 percent of high-school students said that their teachers “often” or “almost daily” told them to be “actively anti-racist”; more than a third said that teachers frequently told them the United States is a fundamentally racist nation. New York City public schools trained administrators and principals using materials claiming that “objectivity,” thinking “in a linear way,” and “worship of the written word” are white ideas. To the extent that these efforts help the drive for privatization, they are producing a terrible outcome, both for public education and for society as a whole. Strong public-school systems require support from across the political spectrum. To shore up that support, they need to take a more neutral ideological posture and reclaim their traditional role in cultivating a universal vision of American citizenship. The timing of the new voucher laws couldn’t be worse for public schools, which are already losing millions of students. This fall, an estimated 3.2 million fewer students will attend public schools than in 2019. That’s in part because Americans are having fewer children, but attrition to private schools even without vouchers is a factor as well. Overall, private-school enrollment in America increased by 28 percent from the period prior to the pandemic to 2024. A 2025 Tulane University study of voucher programs in 11 states found that the “lion’s share” of those taking advantage were already in private school, but the authors believed that this would likely change over time. “Vouchers have already increased private school enrollment in participating states by 3-4%” compared with non-voucher states, they noted, and one of the Tulane researchers, Douglas Harris, said that the shift was likely the “tip of the iceberg.” Arizona made a voucherlike program universal in 2022. State data show that only 21 percent of participants in the program in the 2023 fiscal year had switched from public schools; by 2025, that proportion had increased to 56 percent. The trend toward private schools is likely to accelerate. Under Donald Trump, a Republican Congress passed a new federal tax credit that subsidizes private educational services, including tutoring and private-school tuition, for students from families that make up to 300 percent of the local median gross income—a standard that includes more than 90 percent of the K–12 population. Individuals who donate up to $1,700 to a nonprofit scholarship-granting organization receive a dollar-for-dollar credit on their federal tax returns—costing them nothing. SGOs then provide aid for students. The law, which takes effect in January, could generate $24 billion or more in spending, supporters estimate . The new credit could exceed the $18 billion the federal government invests in Title I, the biggest federal program for public K–12 education. Public-school students who use private tutors may share in benefits, but the bulk of the money will likely support private schools. “This is a private school choice program that might benefit public school students at the margins,” my Progressive Policy Institute colleague Rachel Canter has argued . The legendary 20th-century teachers’-union leader Albert Shanker, the son of Russian Jewish immigrants, recognized that support for public schools hinged on their ability to bring the country together. If schools focus on differences rather than on the commonalities that define students as Americans, he argued , “there will be no reason for taxpayers to continue supporting them.” Public schools long promoted American identity through civics instruction that emphasized the benefits of the country’s liberal democracy, and through U.S-history curricula that leaned heavily—sometimes too heavily—on the successes of American democracy. But civics education has been eroding for decades, and in many districts, history lessons have swung too far in a condemnatory direction. As educators have become more attuned to racial injustice, most recently with the rise of the Black Lives Matter movement, they have embraced ideas pushed in education schools that racism and white supremacy are the defining features of America. The National Education Association—the country’s largest teachers’ union and a major force in Democratic politics—got caught up in the ideological ferment on the left and promoted the much-disputed “1619 Project,” which puts slavery at the center of U.S. history and has elicited serious factual objections from prominent historians. These developments carry political risks for public schools: Polling from the American Enterprise Institute shows that 77 percent of adults think that teaching kids that “the U.S. is a fundamentally good country” is “important” or “absolutely essential.” But today, four in 10 Gen Z Americans believe that the Founders were villains rather than heroes. Public educators’ First Amendment rights are not absolute in the classrooms they oversee. Even if their legal right to press their personal views during the school day were undisputed, the educational value of doing so is debatable, and school systems should be cautious about seeming to take sides on political matters. One recent legal dispute involved a Progress Pride flag that a high-school teacher on Long Island had put up in her classroom; it was twice the size of the American flag. Some of the views implied by the Pride flag are barely controversial anymore, at least in blue states. A large majority of Americans, including me, support same-sex marriage and laws prohibiting discrimination against gay and trans people. Even so, the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, in an opinion written by a Joe Biden appointee who is a lesbian, sensibly backed the school district’s position that only the American flag and the New York State flag should be flown in its classrooms. LGBTQ kids deserve reassurance that they are welcome. But a Pride flag is also a political statement, just as a Trump flag or a Blue Lives Matter flag is. Teachers are authority figures, and ideological restraint on their part helps protect public education’s legitimacy before a polarized electorate. At the same time, teaching students what being an American means should be a central goal. This does not mean that schools should teach only an upbeat version of American history. Students need an honest accounting of that history, which includes the subjugation of Black people, women, and gay Americans. But as the Albert Shanker Institute has argued , students should also learn how “the genius of democracy” allows for self-correction. Only because the Constitution guarantees free speech and assembly rights could average citizens partake in successful movements to advance civil rights for Black Americans, women, and gay people. Americans across the political divide are likely to support a middle path. Nine in 10 Democrats want kids to see the Declaration of Independence and Constitution in a positive light, and eight in 10 Republicans want students to learn about slavery and segregation. [ Listen: Testing teachers for ‘wokeness’ ] Schools should also teach more students what it’s like to live in nondemocratic societies. Just as Americans who travel abroad come to more fully appreciate aspects of American culture they took for granted, curricula that touch on life in Iran, Russia, and China will also illuminate what makes the United States different. All students should know what naturalized U.S. citizens and the children of immigrants—two groups that express comparatively higher levels of patriotism—recognize: the difference between American society and societies with less freedom and opportunity. Upholding a common vision of citizenship is essential for the nation’s well-being, and only public schools can do this job. For all their faults, they are more likely than private schools— three-quarters of which are affiliated with a specific religion—to provide the adhesion necessary in a country made up of many races and creeds. The Stanford political scientist Terry Moe, a voucher supporter, has found that Americans have a “ public school ideology ” —that is, they like the idea of institutions that take all comers and teach young people what they have in common as Americans. That’s why voter referendums supporting public money for private schools have typically failed . Voucher advocates’ recent attempts to exploit the culture wars could change all of this—and, if so, could further divide Americans. Public schools can be the answer to the polarization and atomization that so threaten our common life, but only if they fully resume their historic role in binding our multicultural democracy together.

Tunisie | La marche des diplômés chômeurs reprend après un arrêt à Jelma
items.description: La «Marche de la dignité», qui a démarré le 27 septembre 2026 à Menzel Bouzaiane, dans le gouvernorat de Sidi Bouzid, berceau de la révolution du 10 décembre 2010-14 janvier 2011, est une initiative de diplômés au chômage en Tunisie, qui se dirigent à pied vers Carthage, pour réclamer l’application de la loi n° 18 de 2025 relative aux recrutements exceptionnels dans le secteur public. Des proches des chômeurs participent également à cette mobilisation, selon la page officielle de l’Union des diplômés chômeurs (UDC). Cependant, en raison de la détérioration de l’état de santé de plusieurs participants et du fait que la plupart d’entre eux n’avaient plus la capacité physique de poursuivre la marche, ils ont été contraints de faire une halte temporaire, mardi 29 septembre, afin de préserver la sécurité de tous. Certains ont dû soigner leurs blessures aux pieds à l’hôpital régional de Jelma. «Toutefois, cet arrêt ne signifie nullement un renoncement aux revendications, mais constitue une pause imposée par les circonstances. Le mouvement se poursuivra avec la même détermination, pour faire valoir le droit au travail et à la dignité» , dit l’un des organisateurs. Aux dernières nouvelles, les marcheurs et les marcheuses ont repris la route, toujours à pied, à l’aube de ce mercredi 30 septembre, direction Tunis, puis Carthage, au nord de la capitale. Selon Wassim Jeddi, responsable régional de l’UDC, l’objectif est de porter directement auprès de la présidence de la République la demande de mise en œuvre concrète des procédures prévues par la loi. Ce texte, promulgué en décembre 2025, prévoit des recrutements par tranches ainsi qu’une plateforme nationale pour classer les candidats selon des critères liés à l’âge, à l’ancienneté du diplôme et à la situation sociale. Les organisateurs ont appelé les diplômés chômeurs des autres régions à soutenir la marche tout au long du trajet vers la capitale. Toutefois, aucune adhésion organisée à l’échelle nationale ni aucun calendrier officiel des étapes n’ont été signalés pour le moment. Cette contestation survient après l’évacuation, début septembre, d’un sit-in de diplômés chômeurs dans le centre de Tunis, et après des semaines de manifestations dans plusieurs régions du pays pour exiger l’application effective de la loi. Les participants réclament également la libération de Karim Teraâ, figure du mouvement des diplômés chômeurs, arrêté récemment. L’UDC a réclamé dans un communiqué sa libération et l’abandon des poursuites engagées contre lui. Aucun incident ni intervention des forces de sécurité n’a été signalé pour l’instant le long du parcours. Par ailleurs, le secrétaire général de l’Union générale tunisienne du travail (UGTT), Slaheddine Selmi, avait reçu, lundi 28 septembre, une délégation de l’UDC, conduite par son secrétaire général, Cherif Khraifi. Une rencontre consacrée à la situation générale et aux prochaines mobilisations de l’organisation. I. B. items.title: Commerce extérieur : un redressement de la balance commerciale du Sénégal noté en juillet dernier
items.description: Le commerce extérieur du Sénégal est marqué en juillet 2026 par un redressement de la balance commerciale affichant un excédent de 54,9 milliards de francs CFA, contre un déficit de 129,4 milliards de FCFA au mois précédent. C’est ce qui ressort du rapport des repères statistiques rendu public mardi par l’Agence nationale de la statistique et de la démographie (Ansd). En juillet 2026, la balance commerciale du Sénégal se redresse, affichant un excédent de 54,9 milliards de FCFA, contre un déficit de 129,4 milliards de FCFA au mois précédent. Cette évolution est tirée, selon l’Agence nationale de la statistique et de la démographie (Ansd), par une hausse des exportations de 143,5 milliards de FCFA, face à un repli des importations de 40,8 milliards de FCFA en rythme mensuel. Rebond des ventes de pétrole brut de 185,7 milliards de FCFA « La bonne dynamique des exportations s’explique par le rebond des ventes de pétrole brut (+185,7 milliards de FCFA) et, dans une moindre mesure, des autres produits pétroliers (+15,9 milliards de FCFA) ainsi que de l'acide phosphorique (+12,4 milliards de FCFA) », indique l’Ansd dans son rapport des repères statistiques publié mardi. S’agissant des importations, l’agence note que le recul résulte principalement de la baisse des achats de machines et appareils à moteurs à hauteur de 26,5 milliards de FCFA, d'ouvrages en métaux de 15,7 milliards de FCFA. Mais, du recul de l’achat de produits pharmaceutiques de 15,5 milliards de FCFA et de produits céréaliers de 12,3 milliards de FCFA. Ceci, malgré la hausse de celles de produits pétroliers de 71,1 milliards de FCFA et de matériels de transport de 29,1 milliards de FCFA. Comparativement à juillet 2025, le solde commercial s’améliore de 258,6 milliards de FCFA au mois sous revue. 392,0 milliards de FCFA de recettes enregistrés par l’Etat Contrairement au solde commercial, il ressort également du même document qu’au mois sous revue, les recettes totales de l’État se sont réduites. Elles se sont établies à 392,0 milliards de FCFA, contre 545,1 milliards de FCFA en juin 2026, soit une contraction de 28,1% en variation mensuelle. « Cette baisse est imputable à la diminution des recettes fiscales de 164,4 milliards de FCFA, malgré le progrès des recettes non fiscales de 11,3 milliards de FCFA. En glissement annuel, les recettes totales de l’Etat progressent de 5,9%. Ce résultat s’explique par la bonne tenue des recettes fiscales (+4,8%) et non fiscales (+20,9%) », précise l’Ansd. Mariama DIEME

items.title: En Roumanie, le Premier ministre Siegfried Mureșan n’a pas obtenu la confiance du Parlement
items.description: Le Premier ministre désigné, Siegfried Mureșan, n'est pas parvenu à obtenir ce mercredi 30 septembre la confiance du Parlement. Il n'a recueilli que 182 voix, alors que 233 étaient requises. Le président Nicușor Dan a désormais deux options : convoquer des élections anticipées, qu'il a pour l'instant exclues alors que le parti d'extrême droite AUR (Alliance pour l'union des Roumains) est en tête des sondages, ou désigner un nouveau candidat au poste de Premier ministre issu du Parti socialiste démocrate (PSD), le plus probablement, Sorin Grindeanu. Mureșan, député européen issu du PNL et vice-président du PPE, a été nommé à la suite de la chute du gouvernement Bolojan après un vote commun PSD/AUR. Les deux partis disposent ensemble de 218 sièges sur 464 au Parlement. Ces derniers reprochaient au gouvernement ses mesures d'austérité, alors que le déficit roumain était en 2025 le plus élevé de l'Union (7,9 % du PIB). Faute de gouvernement, Bucarest risque désormais de voir sa note souveraine basculer en catégorie spéculative (« junk »). Selon les déclarations de responsables du parti, l’objectif d’AUR est de destituer Nicușor Dan. La procédure suppose un vote à la majorité du Parlement, puis un référendum organisé dans les 30 jours. Depuis l’annulation, en décembre 2024, du premier tour de l’élection présidentielle, la Roumanie est prise dans une double tenaille, avec d’un côté la Russie, et de l’autre les États-Unis. Le pays est ainsi devenu un laboratoire géopolitique de la situation des forces politiques européennes. Călin Georgescu , placé hier, mardi 29 septembre, en détention provisoire pour 30 jours dans une affaire d'escroquerie et de constitution de groupe criminel organisé, avait remporté le premier tour du scrutin avec 22,94 % des voix. Ignoré par la plupart des enquêtes d’opinion et jamais donné au-delà de 8 % des voix, sa campagne électorale avait été menée principalement sur les réseaux sociaux, particulièrement TikTok. Il avait été arrêté en février 2025 suite à l’organisation de 47 perquisitions chez plusieurs de ses proches, alors que le parquet l’accusait de financements occultes de Moscou. Le ministre roumain des Affaires étrangères, Emil Hurezeanu, avait dénoncé « une forme d’ingérence dans les élections internes d’un autre État ». Le parti AUR a déclaré aujourd’hui au Parlement qu'il ne voterait pour aucun gouvernement tant que Călin Georgescu ne serait pas mis en liberté. La Roumanie est d’ailleurs en première ligne de la guerre hybride que Moscou mène en Europe : les avions F-18 de l'armée de l'air espagnole, déployés depuis le mois d'août sur la base de Mihail Kogălniceanu, ont effectué 15 décollages d'urgence au cours de leur premier mois de mission en Roumanie REPORTAJ la Mihail Kogălniceanu : „În 3 săptămâni am avut mai multe alerte ca-n 4 luni, în alte misiuni”. Cum luptă piloții spanioli de F-18 din România contra „încercărilor Rusiei de a testa NATO” », HotNews , 30 septembre 2026.'> 5 . De l’autre côté, les États-Unis exercent des pressions pour influencer les décisions du gouvernement. En mars, Kimberly Guilfoyle, l’ambassadrice américaine en Grèce et ancienne fiancée de Don Jr., le fils aîné du président américain, aurait évoqué lors d'un dîner privé l'effondrement alors imminent du gouvernement roumain, au cours d'un échange avec le ministre grec de l'Énergie, Stavros Papastavrou The Mystery Man Shadowing Kimberly Guilfoyle as She Pushes Deals Across Europe », The Wall Street Journal , 25 septembre 2026.'> 6 . Devant d'autres responsables grecs et américains, elle aurait notamment déclaré : « Nous pouvons faire ça à n'importe quel pays de notre choix. Nous pouvons le faire ici [en Grèce] », suggérant que Washington avait pu jouer un rôle dans la chute du gouvernement quelques semaines plus tard, le 5 mai. Le gouvernement Bolojan aurait été mal perçu à Washington en raison de son refus d'acheter du GNL américain. En juillet, le département d’État américain a lancé un appel à propositions visant à soutenir des organisations politiquement alignées en Europe. Le programme est destiné à financer des projets portés par des ONG, des groupes de réflexion ou des universités, axés sur la liberté d’expression, la souveraineté et les migrations, pour des subventions allant jusqu’à 3 millions de dollars. Son démarrage est prévu aujourd’hui, mercredi 30 septembre. items.title: Los caseros no podrán cobrar más al alquilar un piso por habitaciones que por ofrecerlo entero
items.description: Junto con el endurecimiento de las condiciones para poder firmar un alquiler de temporada , uno de los reales decretos aprobados este martes por el Gobierno en el Consejo de Ministros también modifica las circunstancias relacionadas con el arrendamiento de habitaciones de forma que el propietario no pueda sacar más rentabilidad alquilándolo por habitaciones que si lo hiciera como piso completo. Una modalidad que, pese a que no existe un registro oficial que permita comprobar su evolución, distintos estudios que han analizado la oferta existente en los portales inmobiliarios de referencia apuntan a que se ha encarecido sobremanera en los últimos años. Hasta el punto de que, según un análisis de Pisos.com, alquilar una habitación se come casi un tercio del sueldo neto de los jóvenes en las ciudades más tensionadas, como Madrid, Barcelona o Valencia. items.title: Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno appelle les Tchadiens de tous horizons à « donner ce qu’ils peuvent » pour la réhabilitation et l’équipement des écoles publiques

items.title: Du lit d’hôtel au-dessous d’un pont: le mystère de la mort tragique d’un amant à Abuja
items.description: À Abuja, au Nigeria, une rencontre intime entre une femme mariée et son amant a viré au drame. La police du Territoire de la Capitale fédérale (FCT) a interpellé Rukayat Muhammed ainsi que deux employés d’un établissement hôtelier, après la découverte du corps de l’homme sous un pont de Katampe. Le commissaire de police, Ahmed Sanusi, qui a révélé les faits, le samedi 26 septembre 2026, souligne que les circonstances exactes de son décès restent à établir. L’affaire, qui a débuté par la découverte d’un corps sous le pont de Katampe, dans la zone de Kubwa, prend une tournure pour le moins troublante à Abuja. Une femme mariée, identifiée comme Rukayat Muhammed, et deux employés d’une maison d’hôtes ont été arrêtés dans le cadre de l’enquête sur la mort d’un homme dont le corps avait été retrouvé abandonné. Le commissaire de police du Territoire de la Capitale fédérale, Ahmed Sanusi, a révélé les faits, le samedi 26 septembre 2026, lors d’un point de presse à Abuja. Selon les premiers éléments communiqués par la police, la victime avait été signalée disparue par sa famille avant que son corps ne soit retrouvé le 26 août dernier, sous le pont de Katampe, le long de la voie express de Kubwa. Une rencontre qui tourne au drame Les investigations policières ont notamment porté sur le téléphone portable du défunt, qui avait disparu. Les enquêteurs auraient ainsi identifié sa dernière interlocutrice, Rukayat Muhammed, résidant à Garki Area 2. La police affirme que la femme mariée entretenait une relation amoureuse avec le défunt. Les deux auraient séjourné ensemble au Good Samaritan Guest House, à Gwarimpa, où l’homme aurait soudainement cessé de respirer. D’après les déclarations du commissaire Sanusi, Rukayat aurait constaté que son compagnon ne respirait plus. Au lieu d’alerter immédiatement les services compétents, elle aurait quitté les lieux avec le téléphone portable du défunt. Quelques heures, plus tard, le personnel de l’établissement, ne parvenant plus à joindre les occupants de la chambre, aurait découvert le corps à l’intérieur. Deux employés, Ibrahim Omeiza et Kefat Bitrus, sont alors soupçonnés par la police d’avoir déplacé le cadavre avant de l’abandonner sous le pont de Katampe. Le mystère demeure sur la cause du décès Malgré les arrestations, la police souligne que la cause exacte et les circonstances précises de la mort n’ont pas encore été établies. L’enquête se poursuit donc afin de déterminer le rôle éventuel de chacun dans le décès, mais aussi dans le déplacement et l’abandon du corps. Les autorités ont également indiqué que toute personne reconnue impliquée dans la mort de la victime ou dans la dissimulation de son corps devra répondre de ses actes devant la justice. De la chambre d’une maison d’hôtes au bord d’une route sous un pont, l’affaire laisse encore plusieurs questions sans réponse. Les investigations de la police d’Abuja devront notamment déterminer ce qui s’est réellement passé durant les dernières heures de la victime et pourquoi son corps a été déplacé puis abandonné. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Du lit d'hôtel au-dessous d'un pont: le mystère de la mort tragique d'un amant à Abuja est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Gabon : 96 % des subventions à l’essence et au gasoil profitent aux plus aisés, selon la Banque mondiale
items.description: Au Gabon, « les subventions aux carburants ne sont pas bien ciblées », selon la Banque mondiale, qui relève dans sa Revue des finances publiques du Gabon 2026, publiée le 29 septembre, que ces aides, destinées notamment à atténuer le coût de la vie, profitent principalement aux ménages les plus aisés. L'institution préconise une réforme progressive, accompagnée de mécanismes de compensation mieux ciblés. Au Gabon, 96 % des subventions à l’essence et au gasoil profitent aux plus aisés, selon la Banque mondiale. © D.R. Les subventions aux carburants constituent une charge importante pour les finances publiques gabonaises. Dans sa dernière revue consacrée au pays, la Banque mondiale estime qu’elles « ne sont pas bien ciblées » . Selon ses estimations, 96 % du coût des subventions à l’essence et au gasoil bénéficient à la moitié la plus aisée de la population. 1 % du PIB consacré aux carburants Le poids budgétaire de ce dispositif est également mis en avant. En 2024, les subventions aux carburants ont représenté 1 % du PIB, soit un niveau comparable à l’ensemble de l’allocation nationale destinée à la santé et supérieur à un tiers du budget de l’éducation, établi à 2,9 % du PIB. Pour la Banque mondiale, cette allocation présente un coût d’opportunité important. Les subventions favorisent fortement les groupes à revenus élevés et profitent à la consommation de produits importés. L’institution estime ainsi qu’elles contribuent peu à une croissance inclusive tout en réduisant les marges disponibles pour d’autres dépenses sociales. Une réduction progressive plutôt qu’une suppression brutale Cependant, la Banque mondiale ne préconise pas une suppression immédiate du dispositif. Elle propose plutôt une réforme graduelle et déterminée, assortie de mesures destinées à protéger les populations vulnérables. La première condition avancée est la mise en place d’un registre social solide, permettant de mieux identifier les bénéficiaires des dispositifs publics. Les économies dégagées par la réduction des subventions pourraient ensuite être réorientées vers des transferts monétaires ciblés, ainsi que vers la santé primaire et l’éducation. Un soutien ciblé pour les transporteurs L’institution identifie également la question du transport comme un enjeu particulier. Les taxis, y compris les taxis informels, sont utilisés par une large partie de la population. Elle suggère donc des mesures d’atténuation ciblées et limitées dans le temps pour certains secteurs, notamment les transporteurs, avec entre autres l’immatriculation des taxis informels. Sur le plan budgétaire, la Loi de finances initiale pour 2026 prévoyait de ramener le coût des subventions aux carburants à 12 milliards de FCFA, contre un objectif porté à 55 milliards de FCFA dans la Loi de finances révisée, soit environ 0,4 % du PIB. Selon la Banque mondiale, les réformes envisagées n’avaient toutefois pas encore été adoptées en juillet 2026. La Banque mondiale estime qu’une telle réforme, combinant réduction progressive des subventions, ciblage social et soutien aux ménages vulnérables, permettrait de dégager des marges budgétaires tout en réorientant davantage les ressources publiques vers les dépenses sociales. L’article Gabon : 96 % des subventions à l’essence et au gasoil profitent aux plus aisés, selon la Banque mondiale est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Compte unique trésor : l’État recherche ses milliards dispersés
items.description: © DR Près de 450 milliards de FCFA de ressources publiques dormaient dans les banques commerciales en 2022. Quatre ans plus tard, le ministre des Finances Louis Paul Motaze lance le 29 septembre 2026 à Yaoundé un nouvel atelier de recensement pour actualiser ces chiffres et accélérer la centralisation au Trésor. Objectif : plus de visibilité, plus de transparence. Yaoundé. Le ministre des Finances, Louis Paul Motaze, a réuni le 29 septembre 2026 banquiers, assureurs et administrations publiques autour d'un enjeu stratégique : le Compte Unique du Trésor (CUT). Lancée en 2022, la réforme avait alors révélé l'ampleur du phénomène : près de 450 milliards de FCFA appartenant à l'État et à ses démembrements étaient dispersés dans les banques commerciales, hors du contrôle direct du Trésor public. Quatre ans après, le gouvernement veut voir clair. Cette opération d'actualisation vise à recenser avec précision tous les comptes des administrations publiques encore ouverts dans le circuit bancaire, leur solde exact et leur mode de gestion. Pourquoi cet exercice est-il crucial ? Pour le MINFI, sans recensement, pas de centralisation efficace. Il s'agit de savoir où se trouve l'argent public, à combien il s'élève et comment il est utilisé. Les gains attendus du CUT sont majeurs : une meilleure visibilité sur la trésorerie de l'État, une programmation plus efficace des dépenses, une réduction des besoins d'emprunt à court terme et surtout une sécurisation des fonds. Pour le citoyen, l'impact est direct. Mieux centraliser les ressources, c'est éviter que des milliards ne dorment dans des comptes peu rémunérés pendant que l'État s'endette à taux élevé. C'est renforcer la capacité de l'État à payer ses prestataires, à financer les hôpitaux, les écoles et les infrastructures. Le CUT, c'est la modernisation de la gestion publique en marche. Cet article Compte unique trésor : l'État recherche ses milliards dispersés est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: The Great Data-Center Rebellion
items.description: Clinton, Iowa, is topographically flat and economically declining. The sawmills that made the city rich in the late 19th century have been repurposed as a museum. One of the Victorian mansions long since abandoned by the old lumber barons is open for tours, but tourists are scarce. Clinton has shrunk to about 24,000 people, and the town center, along the Mississippi River, feels nearly empty. On the west side, miles of deep-green corn and soy fields are crisscrossed with transmission wires and zoned for heavy industrial use. The city’s economic activity includes corn processing, pet-food production, and methamphetamines. With available land and a dire need for investment, Clinton seems like the perfect place for a gigantic data center. In January, a Clintonian named Stephen Figg, who owns a small firm that builds technological infrastructure, including for data centers, heard from a customer that a broker was making inquiries about buying farmland on the west side, north of Highway 30. In mid-February, a father of two girls named Ryan Wisor, who had obtained a residential exemption to live in that area, noticed surveyors with boring rigs working in the field behind the house he’d built. He asked his stepsister, who sits on the city council, if she knew of a planned development. Several weeks later, she told him of a proposal for a data center. He learned that the project would border his house on two sides and come to within 65 feet of his well. For almost two years, city officials, utility companies, and a pro-business nonprofit, Grow Clinton, had been in discussions about the construction of a data center in Clinton. It later emerged that an international developer called Quality Technology Services (QTS), owned by the trillion-dollar private-equity firm Blackstone, planned to build one of the country’s largest AI data centers—10 buildings of 500,000 square feet each—on behalf of a client that remains anonymous. Private meetings, nondisclosure agreements, and even a code name (“Saturday River”) had kept the plan’s existence quiet until Andy Sokolovich, the president of Grow Clinton, unveiled the proposal at a county-board meeting on April 27. He had wanted to keep the project confidential longer, but word was getting out. Theresa Andrews, a quality analyst at a chemical company, had heard a rumor in mid-March about a development planned for the cornfields in her area, but she’d blown it off. After watching the April 27 county meeting online, she went on the city’s website and noticed dozens of requests for information about the status of parcels of farmland; a few of them were right across the street from her house. Andrews stayed up late for several nights creating a spreadsheet of the parcels and then a map of the projected site. The scale was almost unimaginable: 1,100 acres, or 832 football fields—about the size of Central Park. This would be a “hyperscale” data center, and it turned out to be far along. From FOIA requests, Andrews learned that plans for upgrading utilities in the area had been in the works since 2024. This was how the Data-Center Rebellion of 2026 came to Clinton, Iowa. Not through Chinese propaganda, or misinformation on social media—though both are plentiful—but because a small group of residents accidentally got wind of a megaproject planned for their community. Andrews, Wisor, Figg, and others had concerns about water consumption, electrical-grid capacity, soil contamination, low-frequency sound waves, nonstop light, an invasion of out-of-state contractors, and—for those in the leviathan’s shadow—the permanent destruction of their rural life. “There’s no proven history of these things,” Wisor told me. He imagined playing in the yard with his 9-year-old daughter and worrying what their colossal new neighbor might be doing to his family’s health. “I go sit outside and all I think is, This could all be gone . You can’t turn it off.” Large numbers of Clintonians began to attend contentious city-council meetings. On June 9, the council voted down a proposal for a 120-day moratorium that would have allowed more time to assess the risks of something so immense and unknown. The city proceeded to draft an ordinance for a data center’s construction and use. Legally, QTS could begin without one. According to Andrews, city officials “were trying to tell us we have to hurry and get the ordinance in place so QTS won’t just start building: ‘You should want us to push fast.’ ” Instead, she and other citizens formed Clintonians Against Data Centers. Even in a city as small as Clinton, the seven members of the group’s steering committee—four women and three men, all white, most of them middle-aged—were at first strangers to one another. The group includes Republicans and Democrats, probably more of the former, but they didn’t know one another’s political affiliations and didn’t seem to want to. Political comments unrelated to artificial intelligence are scrubbed from the Facebook page. “It’s a fun collection in terms of their politics,” Chris Baldus, the editor of the Clinton Herald , told me. “Outside of this, there’s no way in hell these people are talking to each other.” Celeste Robbins, who works in law enforcement and describes herself as both “artsy” and “very religious,” is a disenchanted Trump voter. “If you want to get rich as a state or as a town,” the president said in September, “you’re going to want a data center.” Robbins told me, “I do not agree with him about this.” She lives far from the proposed site, and her opposition comes down to AI itself: She hates the ease with which it replaces human thought, and she fears the mass elimination of jobs. Figg, who couldn’t bring himself to vote for either candidate in the last presidential election, has worked in tech all his life and welcomes the progress that AI might bring. He had just finished eight months of work on an Amazon data center in Indiana when he learned about the proposal for Clinton. He started attending city-council meetings to offer his expertise. “But the more that I try to provide this knowledge to the city and the city council and the mayor, the less receptive they are,” he told me. “That makes it very difficult for me to want to continue that pursuit instead of the pursuit of just trying to prevent it.” With four children and a small business, Figg had never been involved in local activism before joining Clintonians Against Data Centers. According to a recent NBC poll , nearly 70 percent of Americans oppose the construction of a data center in their area. Kevin Bradley of Clintonians Against Data Centers observed that this many Americans haven’t agreed on anything since 9/11: “This is affecting all of us—rich, middle-class, and poor. We’re coming together because we’re not happy.” More than 500 jurisdictions have passed moratoriums or bans . This grassroots movement rose so fast and spread so widely that politicians in both parties, including Iowa’s candidates for governor and senator, are struggling to catch up with their constituents. The meteoric emergence of the data-center rebellion is a response to the speed and scale of construction, which in turn reflect the sudden ubiquity of generative and agentic AI. President Trump’s policy has been to turn everything about the technology, including data-center construction, over to private industry. He derides people like Robbins, Figg, and Andrews for wanting to remain “backwards and poor.” But on this issue, most of Trump’s base remains angry and opposed to him; the only precedent might be the case of Jeffrey Epstein. By pushing so hard and promising so much, tech companies, venture capitalists, and their political allies ensured that AI would create a firestorm. Supporters of data centers point out the benefits—jobs, tax revenues, the many advantages of AI itself. Clinton’s mayor, Scott Maddasion, told me that the project could bring $20 million in annual property taxes to a city with a $24 million budget. Sokolovich, of Grow Clinton, told me it would be closer to $30 million. He said that QTS has requested no tax incentives and will pay for 100 percent of the utility improvements required for the center to operate. A spokesman for Alliant Energy, the region’s regulated electric utility, promised residents that costs related to the data center’s extreme demand would not fall on existing customers. [ Read: The one town that wants a data center ] Clintonians Against Data Centers was not immune to bad information and conspiracist thinking. One member speculated that the sudden appearance around Clinton this past spring of three giant trolls, sculpted from local reclaimed lumber by the Danish artist Thomas Dambo to commemorate the trees consumed by the sawmills, had been funded by QTS to create a “diversion.” A pro-data-center councilman mocked Robbins when, after touring another QTS project in Cedar Rapids, she reported having seen only one bird. Baldus, the newspaper editor, complained that the opposition doesn’t understand how city government works, “and they come in hot.” Sokolovich analogized data-center opposition to COVID skepticism and election denialism. But the facts about water consumption and tax revenues, though important, are not the crux of the matter. Opposition to data centers comes from a deeper concern than NIMBYism, resource misuse, or environmental harm. Over and over, Clintonians expressed a feeling of being misled, ignored, disrespected, betrayed—of having no say over basic matters in their own lives. The data center seemed to be a deal made among secretive insiders—huge, far-off entities in Silicon Valley, on Wall Street, and in Washington, as well as the local leaders of their own city. To the tech giants, QTS, Blackstone, and the Trump administration’s AI boosters, Clinton is an empty space on the Mississippi that looks like an opportunity. That the industry seeking to buy 1,100 acres on the west side of town is in the business of replacing human beings with machines—and perhaps, according to some AI experts, even rendering them extinct—only intensifies a sense of powerlessness. The data-center rebellion, with its local origins and compounding grievances, is thoroughly American. In the 18th century, rural citizens rose up against heavy taxes and farm seizures. In the early 20th century, a time in many ways similar to our own, Louis Brandeis spoke of the “curse of bigness” : concentrations of money and power so great that the individual almost ceases to exist, and democracy itself is threatened. Like other heartland communities, Clinton has suffered “a history of abandonment,” Matt Parbs, the vice president of Grow Clinton, acknowledged. “Clinton since 1980 has internalized the downturn in midwestern industry.” What if, in a few years, 5 million square feet of steel, concrete, computer servers, and microchips in the cornfields become obsolete and go the way of the sawmills, or of the liberal-arts college in Clinton that was bought by a for-profit, moved entirely online, and closed? I tried to imagine a hyper-scale data center engulfing the yard where Ryan Wisor’s daughter plays with the family’s chickens. Against such an immense force, with all the wealth, political power, technological sophistication, and claims of historical inevitability behind it, a sense of dignity can only raise a small voice in protest. In a city the size of Clinton, the controversy over the data center was bound to hurt personal relationships. Linda Chapman, whose husband was the city’s fire marshal, knows all seven members of the city council and has stopped trusting most of them. Wisor and his stepsister on the council no longer speak. Andy Sokolovich, of Grow Clinton, can’t appear in public without someone sticking a phone camera in his face and asking him incendiary questions. The mayor received a death threat. But the converse is also true: To get anything done, Clintonians can’t just abuse one another on Facebook or podcasts. They have to sit in a room together and talk face-to-face. Throughout the summer, the city pushed ahead with an ordinance while Clintonians Against Data Centers kept raising objections that were mostly ignored, hoping to stall the process until QTS decided to look elsewhere. In early September, I attended a council meeting where the language of the ordinance was to be hammered out. To accommodate several hundred people, the meeting was held not at city hall, but in a cavernous pole-frame lodge at the northern end of the city, in a park overlooking the river. The president and vice president of Grow Clinton were not present. “I don’t want to say I’m intimidated, but the opposition has been vocal,” Sokolovich told me. “I’m growing weary of it.” Baldus, of the Clinton Herald , attended grudgingly, out of professional duty; he didn’t seem to regard coverage of the data center as the most exciting opportunity for his paper. Theresa Andrews, who was routinely staying up past 3 a.m. to research the issues and prepare for meetings, arrived with a tense look on her face and a binder full of scientific studies on topics such as the effects of noise and light on livestock. The seven members of the steering committee, some in green CLINTONIANS AGAINST DATA CENTERS T-shirts, sat at a long table with their backs to the audience, facing Mayor Maddasion, the council, and other city officials. This would be a parley between two groups in which everyone now knew everyone. The mayor, an Air Force veteran in his early 40s with a receding hairline, slender and mild, gaveled the meeting to order and led the room in reciting the Pledge of Allegiance. The meeting went on for more than five hours, while darkness fell over the Mississippi. With a draft of the data-center ordinance on the table in front of him, the mayor briskly led the council members and city officials through it section by section and took their comments. Then he heard out the criticisms and suggestions of Clintonians Against Data Centers. The most contentious issue was setbacks—the required distance between data-center buildings and neighboring residential properties. The draft ordinance called for 1,000 feet. Andrews, quoting a study from counties in Pennsylvania, argued for 1,500 feet—a distance that might make the whole project untenable. A councilman named Cody Seeley, who did most of the talking for the pro-data-center side, said that the developer and property owners could negotiate the setbacks, adding, “I think 500 feet is adequate,” which also happened to be QTS’s position. Cries from the audience of “No! No!” The mayor called for silence. Ryan Wisor, for whom the setback question meant the defense of his homestead, said with a slight quaver in his voice: “My frustration is this ordinance is meant to protect the citizens and our property. This isn’t meant to conform so that we can fit a particular business in a particular piece of land.” He added, “For us to give up our rights, it’s not fair.” General applause. It was the emotional high point of the night. I found the proceedings both mind-numbing and inspiring. The seriousness of purpose, the attention to detail, the stamina required to talk and listen—all of it moved me more than it seemed to impress anyone involved. Clintonians Against Data Centers still felt patronized and ignored. Perhaps the council came away exasperated with the NIMBYs and gadflies who were making the process such an ordeal. (Later, the mayor admitted to me, “We’re learning that there’s probably more ways that we can communicate with the citizens.”) In all likelihood, this small populist uprising will not achieve its goal; a hyperscale data center will come to Clinton, Iowa, amid widespread unhappiness and damaged friendships; and AI will continue to roll over the fields of the republic. But a democratic pulse was still beating along the Mississippi River. That was something. This article appears in the November 2026 print edition with the headline “The Great Data-Center Rebellion.”
